title: Cross-arch memory tiling and router synchronization notes
content:
Summary:
This doc captures a set of ad-hoc experiments and hypotheses around two recurring perf pain points observed when serving long-context workloads across Llama/Mistral/Qwen families: 1) memory tiling / layout mismatches between our allocator/kernels and model-kernel expectations that cause hidden memcpy/device copies, and 2) router synchronization stalls in MoE-style models that amplify interconnect jitter during long KV-cache lifetimes.

Why I care / motivation:
- Customers running 8k+ context workloads (mainly Qwen / Mistral long-context variants) report tail latency spikes and throughput cliffs at scale.
- Root causes look orthogonal to pure compute (kernel speed) — observed behavior points to memory layout and inter-device comms.
- Need cheaper mitigations than full recompile of kernels across every arch; want operational knobs we can expose (tiling config, prefetch windows, router backoff).

Experimental setup (quick notes):
- Nodes: 4xA100-80GB (NVLink) and 8xH100-80GB (DGX-style, tested separately).
- Models: quantized Mistral-30B (4-bit), Llama2-70b-chat QAT (8-bit), Qwen-2-32k (float16 baseline).
- Workloads: synthetic prefix-heavy stream (avg prefix=4k tokens, gen=512), batch sizes 1/4/8 to stress continuous batching and KV cache reuse.
- Tracing: nvprof / Nsight Timeline + custom lightweight per-op timestamps in runtime to correlate application-level router/go-switch events with kernel launches.
- Metrics captured: end-to-end token p95/p99, op-level wall time, PCIe/NVLink utilization, memcpy bytes, number of kernel reuploads/rehashes, router sync wait durations.

Key observations (high-level):
1) Memory tiling mismatch causes ~8–20% extra device-to-device memcpy on certain Qwen kernels.
   - When our allocator uses 256B-aligned tiling vs kernel expecting 512B tile strides, we see a memcpy fallback inside the cuBLAS/cuDNN path reported by Nsight.
   - Effect strongest on H100 with large sequence lengths (>=8k) because scatter/gather patterns cross tile boundaries more frequently.
2) MoE router synchronization (soft barrier) shows micro-slots of 200–700us where a fraction of experts are idle waiting for routable payloads to coalesce; this is amplified by NVLink congestion.
   - On A100 NVLink fabric, spikes are correlated with host-side preemption (kernel eviction due to competing workloads) — results in increased router queueing latency.
3) KV cache longevity (keeping 8k prefix) increases working set pressure leading to periodic icache/memory thrash when our batching merges requests at variable offsets — triggers unexpected tensor copies for alignment.

Representative numbers (averages from the runs):
- Qwen-2-32k (H100): baseline single-token gen latency = 42ms; with mis-tiling enabled (no mitigation) p99=120ms; memcpy bytes per token increased by 18%.
- Mistral-30B (A100): gen latency p95 increased from 36ms -> 48ms under heavy multi-batch (B=8) when router stalls present.
- Llama2-70B (quant8) (H100): observed 9% overhead due to alignment-induced reformatting of attention KV buffers.

Profiling traces & how to reproduce quickly (notes to self):
- Launch server with env: RI_DEBUG_MEM_LAYOUT=1 RI_ROUTER_LOG=1 and run: python tools/rlike_microbench.py --model qwen-2-32k --context 8192 --batch 1 --iters 200
- Capture NVTX ranges and export Nsight timeline. Look for memcpy ranges labeled by driver at the same time as our attention kernel launches.
- Use: nsys profile --trace=nvtx,cuda,osrt -o out %COMMAND%

Hypotheses (root causes):
- H1: Our layout allocator picks page-aligned blocks optimized for max throughput, but some vendor kernels assume fixed tiling/stride for fast vector loads — if stride mismatch, vendor code uses a memcpy staging path.
- H2: Router synchronization uses a coarse-grained software barrier to avoid double-writes to expert buffers; when interconnect latency fluctuates (NVLink congestion or PCIe eviction), the barrier causes queueing that looks like stalls.
- H3: Continuous batching with variable prefix offsets forces our runtime to produce temporary aligned copies to concatenate partial KV slices, which costs extra memory ops and breaks kernel locality.

Mitigations tried (and short results):
- Align allocator to 512B tile boundary: reduced memcpy fallback by ~70% in synthetic kernel runs; end-to-end p99 improved by ~9% on H100. (Patch: allocator/tiling-512b branch.)
- Router softening: changed barrier to per-expert backoff with exponential jitter (experimental): reduced tail stalls but increased variance; net p95 improved but p99 still noisy.
- Prefetch window tuning: prefetching next N=2 KV pages into pinned host memory before kernel launch reduced host->device jitter. Cut copy stalls by ~30% in A100 tests.
- Short-term workaround: expose runtime flag --force-tiling=512 and --router-backoff=exp for customer-facing Dedicated clusters.

Open failures / regressions observed:
- 512B tiling helped H100 but hurt some older kernels on A100 where other assumptions exist — need cross-arch guard.
- Router backoff increases CPU spin time on the host for very high-concurrency scenarios; need to rate-limit.

Actionable next steps (prioritized):
1) Roll allocator tiling option behind runtime feature flag; add automatic detection heuristic (probe small kernel kernel_probe to check memcpy vs fast path). (Owner: Marco)
2) Implement per-expert adaptive backoff in router with cap on CPU spin and measure cost/benefit across A100/H100 clusters. (Owner: Aisha)
3) Add microbench harness that varies prefix offsets to quantify temporary-copy frequency and add unit tests to prevent regressions. (Owner: Diego)
4) Draft a short KB for solutions/ops: 'If p99 spikes on long-context, try --force-tiling=512 and --router-backoff=exp' — for Dedicated customers while we stabilize automatic heuristics. (Owner: Sana)

Notes / To-do (informal):
- Need to get a second pass from FW/kernel team re: vendor kernel expectations. Tagging internal kernel contacts.
- Validate feature flag in a canary Dedicated cluster before wider rollout.
- Add test to CI that runs a small long-context scenario on both A100/H100 images (nightly smoke).

Links / references:
- GH patch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1214 (tiling allocator)
- Slack thread: #eng-runtime thread id 3f5a for live traces and raw Nsight exports
- Related Jira: JIRA-RI-842 (router stalls, long-context)

Appendix — quick heuristics checklist for SRE/on-call:
- If the customer is on H100 and seeing p99 spikes with long prefix -> check RI_DEBUG_MEM_LAYOUT logs for memcpy fallback and try --force-tiling=512 (canary first).
- If spikes appear correlated with other co-hosted workloads -> suspect interconnect contention; try isolating node or moving to Dedicated pool.
- If MoE model shows variance on tail -> enable router-backoff and monitor CPU spin.

Questions left (for the team):
- Can we programmatically detect vendor-kernel memcpy fallback quickly on startup? How expensive will that probe be?
- Is there a hybrid tiling strategy (per-layer or per-op) that avoids global regressions across A100/H100?
- Any objection from infra/security to exposing tiling/routing knobs to customers?

End notes: this is a working doc. Many TODOs. Will update after next canary run (planned 2026-02-15).
